long_biography.plain_text:
An Emil Nolde watercolour acquired in 1972 became the starting point for Reinhold Würth's collection of modern and contemporary art. It now contains more than 20,000 works spanning roughly five centuries. Würth placed museums inside company sites and opened the collection to the public without admission charges. Five company-owned museums and ten associated galleries across Europe have received more than eleven million visits.

Würth and his wife Carmen also established the charitable Würth Foundation in 1987. Based in Künzelsau and focused principally on the surrounding Hohenlohe region, it supports art and culture, education, science and research, and the integration of people with disabilities. Its programmes include schools, cultural institutions, prizes and scholarships.

uncertainties: Forbes labels Würth's fortune self-made, but the documented core asset was the father-founded family business that he inherited at 19. The repository taxonomy therefore uses Inherited and expanded, which captures both the transfer and his exceptional material contribution.

Manufacturing is used because Forbes classifies the fortune around fasteners and calls Würth a hardware manufacturer, while the group defines its core as development, production and sale of fastening and assembly materials. Some first-party histories also call it a trading company, but trade remains tied to the same industrial product platform.

German-language Wikipedia and independent reporting state that Würth later acquired Austrian citizenship. No first-party or government source confirming current dual nationality was found, so the blank secondary-nationality field is not proposed.
No reliable public source established a middle name. Honorary degrees and the title Professor are not entered as a middle name or optional title.
